sentences.text: 9. POINT NO.1:

It is the case of the prosecution that, accused persons borrowed Rs.60 lacs from CW1 and thereafter gave a cheque pertaining to an account which was closed and later, filed a false complaint against CW1 before Halasuru Police Station.
Prosecution in order to prove its case, got examined one witness, the informant as PW1 and got marked three documents as Ex.P1 to Ex.P3.
Ex.P1 is the complaint, Ex.P2 is the Spot mahazar and Ex.P3 is the statement of PW1.
10. CW1, the informant/victim is examined as PW1.
he deposed that, accused persons are known to him.
He was previously working in Alliance University, and accused No. 2 is the Chancellor of the said university.
He deposed that, accused persons did not cheat him in any way.
The financial transaction between the accused persons and himself is now cleared.
The accused did not take money from him with an intention to cheat.
He also deposed that he did not file any complaint against the accused persons in the police station that they had cheated him.
Though PW1 identified his signatures on Ex.P1 and Ex.P2.
Though he was treated as hostile by the prosecution nothing was elicited in this cross-examination and denied that accused cheated him or gave a false complaint against him.
11. On perusal, the prosecution had to prove that the accused gave a cheque of a bank account which was closed, towards repayment of borrowed amount of Rs.60,00,000/- to CW1 and thereby cheated him.
In order to attract the offence u/s 420 of IPC, the prosecution has to prove that there was dishonest intention to cheat CW1 at the beginning of the transaction.
According to CW1, he was hired by the accused persons to work in their university and though there was a financial transaction, accused never intended to cheat him.
It is also submitted that their dispute is resolved and accused never cheated him.
Further, CW1 also denied that the accused gave a complaint against him, with an intent to injure him.
12. As the sole witness who is also the victim turned hostile, there is no iota of evidence to attract the offence alleged by the prosecution.
As such examination of the prosecution witnesses only for the purpose of completing the procedural aspect will not serve any judicious purpose and is sheer waste of the precious time of the Court.

At this stage, it is relevant to rely upon the decision of Satish Mehra v. Delhi Administration and Another, (1996) 9 SCC 766, wherein, the Hon'ble Apex Court has held as follows:
"When the judge is fairly certain that there is no prospect of the case ending in conviction the valuable time of the court should not be wasted for holding a trial only for the purpose of formally completing the procedure to pronounce the conclusion on the future date."

Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case, it is clear that the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubts.
Under these facts and circumstances of the case, the Point No.1 is answered in the Negative.
